text: Good evening. Aurelio Mendoza. Thirty-four years a union pipefitter in this city's boiler rooms, and now president of the Club Jerez: forty-two families from Jerez, in Zacatecas. We meet Thursdays in the parish hall. $ Last year we put a new roof on the clinic in my hometown. No grants. Raffles, a dance, plates of food after Mass. And since 2006 the Club keeps its own fund for lawyers, because we learned in '96 what happens when Washington gets nervous. $ [guarded] So when I hear what is coming now, the raids, the checkpoints, I am not surprised. Nobody my age in this room is surprised. These are not new policies. They are old ones with a new name. What protects our families is not a speech. It is each other.

_to the moderator_ What do I want from the next governor? Less than the others, maybe. Don't send us programs with a clipboard. Every time the city gives a little, somebody comes back later for the names. If the state wants to help, let each community run its own things its own way: its own fund, its own hall, its own hours at the clinic in its own language, without reporting who came. $ [neutral] And to the young people here: put your time where your family is. Come on Thursday. Learn the treasurer's job. The people across Grand mean well, most of them. But when your cousin needs a lawyer at two in the morning, they are not the ones who answer the phone.

Good evening. Aurelio Mendoza, president of the Club Jerez. Forty-two families, Thursdays in the parish hall. Thirty-four years I worked under this city's buildings, so I know where the pipes go. $ Everybody is happy with the president, I see. Good. But I want to say how he got there. Not because Washington woke up kind one morning. Because families like ours registered, knocked on doors, and drove the grandmothers to vote. The Club alone drove forty cars out of the parish parking lot on election day. $ [warm] That is the lesson. A community that holds together, that keeps its own money and its own counsel, puts presidents like this one in office. A community that scatters gets the other kind. I have seen both.

_to the moderator_ What should the next governor do? Remember the forty cars. When the state has money, give it to the communities directly and let them decide. We built a roof in Jerez with no help from anybody; imagine what forty-two families do with a little. Don't make us stand in line behind a program designed somewhere else. $ [guarded] And young people, listen. This good year will not last by itself. Presidents change, four years, eight years. What stays is the room where your people meet. If you want more presidents like this one, the power is not across Grand. It is in your own community, organised, paying in every month, voting together. Build that, and they will come to you.
Everybody's friend. Good. Just remember a bridge needs ground at both ends, and somebody has to keep ours.
You'd have us all be Raymond. I won't argue with you tonight. Come Thursday and argue with me there.
That's it. What's ours, we keep ours. Thursday, sit with the young ones. You've earned the chair.
You kept your own counsel. Not bad. Now come to the hall and tell us what you really think.
A little of everything. You're young, you can do that. Come Thursday anyway, {playerName}.
